analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus operates in the right India consumption sector with solid 15% revenue CAGR, but a 50.9x P/E on an 8.8% ROE business is simply too expensive for what is structurally a thin-margin retail operation. Until valuations correct meaningfully or ROE crosses 15%+, this is not a Jhunjhunwala-style conviction bet.
key_strengths: Revenue scaling well — 15.1% CAGR over 9 years from ₹1,733 Cr to ₹6,136 Cr, with operating profit growing at 33% CAGR — shows operating leverage kicking in
FY25 FCF explosion to ₹482 Cr (from near-zero in prior years) and OCF positive 5/5 years signals improving capital efficiency as store network matures

Right sector — India's pharmacy retail is highly fragmented; organized chains like MedPlus benefit from GST compliance pressure on kiranas, rising branded medicine consumption, and diagnostic integration
key_risks: Valuation completely disconnected from returns — 50.9x P/E for 8.8% ROE and 4.75% operating margin leaves zero margin of safety; any earnings miss will be punishing

Structural margin ceiling — pharmacy retail globally earns thin margins, and deep-pocketed competitors (Reliance/Netmeds, Tata/1mg, Apollo Pharmacy) are aggressively buying market share with loss-leading pricing

Promoter holding at 40.29% is below my 50% comfort threshold, and D/E at 0.65 with borrowings growing from ₹477 Cr to ₹1,193 Cr over 5 years signals capital-hungry expansion that hasn't yet translated into adequate equity returns
red_flags: ROE of 8.8% and ROCE of 10.3% — both below my minimum 15% threshold — at a 50.9x P/E is a fundamental misvaluation
Net profit history is deeply volatile: ₹42 Cr → ₹2 Cr → ₹63 Cr → ₹95 Cr → ₹50 Cr — not the steady compounder I seek
Promoter holding below 50% is uncomfortable in Indian retail context where governance and capital allocation decisions can go wrong quickly
analysis.detailed_analysis:
MedPlus presents a classic Indian retail pharmacy story — large network, right sector, and decent topline momentum. Revenue has compounded at 15.1% over 9 years while EBITDA grew at 30.9%, suggesting the business does have operating leverage as stores mature. The FY25 numbers are genuinely encouraging: net profit of ₹150 Cr (up from ₹66 Cr), FCF of ₹482 Cr, and capex dropping to ₹59 Cr as the network enters harvest mode rather than aggressive expansion. Diagnostic integration and private-label manufacturing are sensible diversification moves.

However, as someone who built wealth by finding businesses where price, quality, and growth all align, MedPlus fails the value test badly. An 8.8% ROE at 50.9x earnings means I am paying 5.8x book for a business that earns less than a fixed deposit rate on its equity. Operating margins at 4.75% leave almost no buffer against competitive attack, and with Reliance and Tata both building pharmacy ecosystems with deep pockets, margin compression is more likely than expansion. I need to see ROE cross 18-20%, margins expand toward 6-7%, and the P/E fall to the 25-30x range before MedPlus becomes interesting. Watch it, but do not own it at these levels.
